title: Trail Crew: East Bay Hills Maintenance
description: Swing a Pulaski and help keep miles of East Bay trails in shape. Monthly work parties tackle drainage, tread repair, and blowdown removal alongside park rangers.
fullDescription: East Bay Regional Park District's volunteer trail crew meets monthly at rotating trailheads across the Oakland and Castro Valley hills. Work parties focus on erosion control, water bar clearing, tread restoration, and invasive plant removal on heavily trafficked routes like Skyline National Trail and the Chabot Loop. Rangers provide all hand tools, gloves, and safety briefings. Volunteers should wear sturdy boots and bring water and lunch. This is physical outdoor work that trail runners, hikers, and mountain bikers especially appreciate.
nextSteps: Register at ebparks.org/volunteer. An Earth Day volunteer event is scheduled for April 25, 2026.

title: Presidio Native Plant Restoration
description: Restore native coastal scrub and dune habitat in the Presidio by removing invasive species and planting locally grown seedlings alongside park conservancy staff.
fullDescription: The Presidio Trust and Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy run one of the most ambitious urban habitat restoration programs in the country. Monthly volunteer stewardship days tackle French broom, Himalayan blackberry, and ice plant across the Presidio's 1,500 acres. Crews work in the dunes near Crissy Field, along the El Polin Loop, and on the Tennessee Hollow watershed. Conservancy staff lead every session, teaching volunteers to identify invasive vs. native plants as they work. All tools provided; wear layers and sun protection.
nextSteps: Register for an upcoming stewardship day at parksconservancy.org/volunteer/community-volunteer-programs. No advance training needed — new volunteers always welcome.

title: Ocean Beach Cleanup Crew
description: Join the Surfrider crew on the first Sunday of each month to collect trash and ghost gear from Ocean Beach before it washes out to sea.
fullDescription: Surfrider Foundation's SF Chapter holds monthly beach cleanups at Ocean Beach, one of the longest urban beaches in the U.S. and a persistent litter hotspot. Volunteers fan out across designated sections, collecting single-use plastics, fishing line, cigarette butts, and occasional ghost gear. All bags, gloves, and pickup tools are provided at the trailhead parking lot. Data is logged for Surfrider's national ocean pollution tracking program. The event is family-friendly and takes about two hours. Stick around afterward — the crew usually grabs coffee at a nearby café.
nextSteps: Check the events calendar at sf.surfrider.org/calendar for upcoming cleanup dates. No pre-registration required — just show up.

title: Shorebird Nest Monitor
description: Monitor snowy plover and Forster's tern nesting sites along the East Bay shoreline from April through August, recording clutch counts and disturbance events.
fullDescription: Golden Gate Bird Alliance coordinates a network of volunteer nest monitors at Eastshore State Park and Albany Mudflat from early April through late August each year. Monitors walk assigned transects on weekend mornings, recording nest locations, egg and chick counts, and any human or predator disturbances using standardized data sheets. All protocols are taught at a free training workshop in late March. Binoculars and data sheets provided; volunteers should bring a spotting scope if they have one. This data directly informs habitat management decisions by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.
nextSteps: Attend the spring training workshop in late March — email Ruth to register. Monitors are asked to cover a minimum of 8 weekends across the season.

title: Save the Bay: Shoreline Habitat Planting
description: Plant pickleweed, cordgrass, and other native marsh plants along the Oakland shoreline to restore tidal wetlands that protect the Bay from sea level rise.
fullDescription: Save the Bay runs the largest tidal wetland restoration program in San Francisco Bay, planting hundreds of thousands of native marsh plants each year with the help of volunteers. This one-day planting event at the Arrowhead Marsh unit in Martin Luther King Jr. Regional Shoreline will install cordgrass and pickleweed plugs into prepared mudflat terrain. Participants should wear clothes they don't mind getting muddy and bring rubber boots if possible (loaners available in limited sizes). Staff botanists lead orientation and guide the planting technique. A great event for first-time volunteers and families.
nextSteps: Register at savesfbay.org/calendar. Additional planting events are scheduled throughout spring and summer 2026.

title: Mt. Tamalpais Trail Steward
description: Help maintain the iconic trails of Mt. Tamalpais — clearing vegetation, building water bars, and protecting sensitive chaparral habitat used by hikers, bikers, and equestrians alike.
fullDescription: One Tam's trail stewardship program coordinates volunteer work parties across the 42,000-acre Tamalpais watershed. Monthly events are led by experienced crew leaders from the Marin County Parks, State Parks, and MMWD. Work typically involves brushing trail margins, installing erosion control structures, and clearing drainage on routes like the Dipsea Trail, Matt Davis Trail, and Coastal Trail. Volunteers are treated to sweeping views of the Marin coast and often encounter hawks, deer, and newts. Tools, gloves, and safety briefings provided. Boots and sun protection required.
nextSteps: Sign up for a work party at onetam.org/volunteer. Habitat restoration events are held monthly — upcoming dates include April 18 and May 16, 2026 (9am–12pm).

title: Elephant Seal Docent — Año Nuevo
description: Guide visitors through the elephant seal colony at Año Nuevo State Park, sharing natural history and ensuring the animals' safety during pupping and molting seasons.
fullDescription: Año Nuevo State Park hosts the largest mainland breeding colony of northern elephant seals in the world. Volunteer docents lead permitted tour groups across the dunes from December through May, interpreting seal behavior, life history, and conservation challenges. POST partners with California State Parks to train and coordinate the volunteer docent corps. Training is an intensive two-day workshop in late November. Docents are asked to commit to at least one weekend day per week during the season. A remarkable experience — you'll stand within feet of 2,000-pound bulls and newborn pups.
nextSteps: Apply by October 31 to attend the November training weekend. Submit your application at openspacetrust.org/volunteer.

title: Marine Mammal Care Volunteer
description: Assist veterinary staff with the feeding, cleaning, and monitoring of rescued harbor seals, California sea lions, and elephant seals at our Marin Headlands hospital.
fullDescription: The Marine Mammal Center is the world's largest marine mammal hospital, rescuing over 1,000 animals per year from Alaska to Baja California. Animal care volunteers are the heart of daily operations: they prepare fish diets, hand-feed pups, clean pools, collect behavioral observations, and assist vets during procedures. The commitment is serious — volunteers complete a multi-session training program and commit to the same 6-hour shift every week for a minimum of six months. In exchange, you'll develop deep knowledge of marine mammal medicine and ecology. Limited spots available; apply early.
nextSteps: Submit a volunteer application at marinemammalcenter.org/get-involved/volunteer/sausalito. Animal care positions require a minimum 6-month weekly commitment to the same shift.

title: Coyote Hills Wetland Restoration
description: Remove invasive pampas grass and salt cedar from ancient tule marshes at Coyote Hills, one of the Bay's best-preserved wetland complexes.
fullDescription: Coyote Hills Regional Park preserves 1,200 acres of Bay wetlands that have sustained human communities for over 2,000 years. Today, invasive plants threaten the tule, bulrush, and pickleweed communities that harbor rails, bitterns, and rare invertebrates. Monthly volunteer restoration days focus on cutting, bagging, and removing pampas grass clumps and salt cedar along marsh edges, followed by replanting with locally grown native sedges and rushes. Park naturalists provide plant ID training and lead discussions on wetland ecology. Tools and gloves provided; bring waders or rubber boots if you have them.
nextSteps: Register online at ebparks.org/get-involved/volunteer and select Coyote Hills work party dates. Events fill quickly — sign up at least two weeks in advance.

title: San Francisco Bay Water Quality Monitor
description: Collect water samples at designated Bay shoreline stations and enter data into a citizen science database tracking pollution, salinity, and nutrient levels over time.
fullDescription: Save the Bay's volunteer water quality monitoring program generates long-term data on Bay health at sites from Coyote Creek to San Pablo Bay. Trained monitors visit assigned stations monthly, collecting water samples, measuring dissolved oxygen and turbidity with field instruments, and recording observations about shoreline litter and wildlife activity. Data is submitted electronically and incorporated into Save the Bay's advocacy reports to the San Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality Control Board. A two-hour online training is required before your first monitoring visit. Equipment is loaned to all active monitors.
nextSteps: Complete the online training at savesfbay.org/monitor and request an equipment kit. You'll be assigned a monitoring station within two weeks.

title: Peninsula Creek Restoration Crew
description: Restore native riparian vegetation along San Francisquito Creek in Palo Alto, creating habitat corridors for steelhead trout, great blue herons, and songbirds.
fullDescription: Grassroots Ecology focuses on restoring the creek and wetland ecosystems of the Santa Clara Valley. Their monthly creek restoration events along San Francisquito Creek in East Palo Alto and Palo Alto combine invasive removal (giant reed, English ivy, and Himalayan blackberry) with replanting of willows, sedges, and native forbs. Grassroots ecologists lead plant identification walks before each work session. The creek corridor provides critical habitat connectivity between the Bay and the Santa Cruz Mountains. All tools and native plants provided; youth volunteers age 12 and older are welcome with a parent or guardian.
nextSteps: Browse upcoming events and register at grassrootsecology.org/calendar. Prior registration required for all events.

title: Bay Area Ridge Trail Builder
description: Work alongside trail professionals to build new sections of the 550-mile Bay Area Ridge Trail, connecting parklands from the North Bay to the South Bay.
fullDescription: The Bay Area Ridge Trail is a 550-mile vision trail linking over 75 parks along the ridgelines surrounding the Bay. The Ridge Trail Council coordinates volunteer construction crews working with professional trail builders to complete missing segments. Monthly work parties tackle tasks ranging from bench cutting on new tread to installing drainage structures and brushing sidehill sections. This is skilled, physical work. Crew leaders provide training in proper tool use and trail construction techniques. Volunteers must be able to hike to remote worksites with a 20 lb pack. Hard hats and tools provided.
nextSteps: Sign up for upcoming trail crew days at ridgetrail.org/volunteer. New participants should read the Trail Crew FAQ before registering.

title: Coastal Trail Litter Cleanup — Marin Headlands
description: Spend a Saturday morning collecting litter along the Coastal Trail in the Marin Headlands, keeping one of the most dramatic stretches of the GGNRA clean for hikers and wildlife.
fullDescription: The Marin Headlands attract hundreds of thousands of visitors each year, and despite most visitors' best intentions, litter accumulates along the most popular coastal routes. This one-time cleanup event focuses on a 4-mile segment of the Coastal Trail from Rodeo Beach to the Wolf Ridge junction. Volunteers split into small teams and work their way up the trail, filling bags with trash and micro-litter. Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy staff lead the event and provide all supplies. The route involves about 600 feet of elevation gain — wear sturdy shoes and bring plenty of water. Spectacular views guaranteed.
nextSteps: Register at parksconservancy.org/volunteer. Parking is limited at Rodeo Beach — carpooling encouraged.

title: Outdoor Naturalist Education Docent
description: Lead school groups on guided nature walks through Tilden Regional Park, teaching students about Bay Area ecology, geology, and wildlife through hands-on outdoor activities.
fullDescription: The East Bay Regional Park District's Tilden Nature Area hosts over 20,000 school children each year through its environmental education program. Volunteer naturalist docents lead 90-minute walks for groups from kindergarten through 6th grade, using inquiry-based activities to explore topics like bird adaptations, plant communities, soil science, and creek ecosystems. Docents receive a 30-hour training course covering ecology content, facilitation skills, and child safety protocols. After training, volunteers commit to one weekday walk per week during the school year. Some of the most rewarding volunteering in the Bay Area — kids are endlessly surprising.
nextSteps: Apply for the next docent training cohort at ebparks.org/tilden-nature. Training runs September–November; applications due August 15.

title: Street Tree Planting — SF Mission District
description: Plant new street trees along Valencia and 24th Street corridors in the Mission, helping reduce urban heat and improve air quality in one of SF's most vibrant neighborhoods.
fullDescription: Friends of the Urban Forest has planted over 55,000 street trees across San Francisco since 1981. Each planting event installs 10–20 trees along a designated block, with volunteers doing all the digging, soil amendment, and mulching under the guidance of certified arborists. The Mission planting focuses on heat-tolerant species like London plane and Chinese pistache that will provide shade for the neighborhood's pedestrians and cyclists for generations. No experience necessary — all tools and materials provided. Lunch served after the planting.
nextSteps: Browse upcoming plantings and RSVP at fuf.net/plantings. Each event is standalone — no ongoing commitment required.

title: Pelagic Bird Survey — Point Reyes
description: Join a research team conducting standardized seabird counts from the Point Reyes Headlands, contributing to long-term population data on murres, shearwaters, and alcids.
fullDescription: Golden Gate Bird Alliance coordinates quarterly pelagic bird surveys at Point Reyes Headlands in partnership with the Point Reyes Bird Observatory. Survey teams of 3–4 volunteers spend 6 hours at the headlands during peak migration windows, recording seabird species, numbers, and behaviors using standardized distance-sampling protocols. Common species include common murre, Brandt's cormorant, Cassin's auklet, and black-footed albatross. Volunteers receive a pre-survey training on identification cues and counting protocol. Spotting scope required (loaners available for first-timers). This is citizen science at its most impactful — the data informs federal fisheries management.
nextSteps: Email Ruth to be added to the survey volunteer pool. Surveys are scheduled based on weather windows — flexibility is important.

title: Estuary Kayak Trash Patrol
description: Paddle kayaks through Islais Creek and Mission Creek channels to collect floating trash and document pollution sources in SF's urban waterways.
fullDescription: SF Rec & Parks partners with local kayak clubs to run monthly paddle cleanups in the city's urban creeks and marina channels. Volunteers use sit-on-top kayaks (provided) to access shallow areas unreachable by foot, scooping up floating plastic, fishing gear, and debris. The route covers Islais Creek from Cesar Chavez to Third Street and portions of Mission Creek near McCovey Cove. No kayaking experience required — a 15-minute orientation covers basic paddling and safety. Participants must be able to swim and are required to wear a PFD throughout. Data on trash quantity and type is submitted to the SF Estuary Institute.
nextSteps: Register at sfrecpark.org/volunteer at least one week before the event. Equipment is provided but space is limited to 12 participants.

title: Marin Open Space Trail Patrol
description: Hike or mountain bike designated trail patrol routes through Marin's open space preserves, providing visitor assistance and reporting maintenance needs and wildlife sightings.
fullDescription: The Marin County Open Space District manages 34 preserves covering more than 17,000 acres of open space across the county. Volunteer trail patrol ambassadors are the eyes and ears of these preserves. Patrols carry a radio and basic first aid kit, assist visitors with maps and regulations, document trail conditions (washouts, blowdown, erosion), and report wildlife observations including mountain lion sightings. Patrols are conducted solo or in pairs and are logged on a standard form submitted after each outing. Patrol volunteers attend a half-day orientation and commit to one patrol per month. Hiking patrols and mountain bike patrols both needed.
nextSteps: Apply at parks.marincounty.gov/discoverlearn/volunteer. Orientations are held quarterly in San Rafael.

title: Acterra Nature Explorers Leader
description: Lead hands-on environmental education activities for Palo Alto elementary students, exploring local creek ecosystems and native plant gardens at Barron Park and Foothills Park.
fullDescription: Acterra's Nature Explorers program brings environmental science alive for K–5 students in Palo Alto Unified School District. Volunteer leaders visit classrooms once a month to conduct inquiry-based activities — from building bug hotels and testing creek water quality to conducting plant surveys and learning to identify common local birds by song. Each lesson connects to California science standards and includes a short outdoor component when possible. Acterra provides all lesson plans, materials, and a two-session leader training. Leaders commit to one classroom visit per month during the school year.
nextSteps: Apply at acterra.org/volunteer by September 1 to join the fall cohort. Leader training is held in late September.

title: Coastal Bluff Invasive Removal — Marin Headlands
description: Remove invasive ice plant from coastal bluffs above Rodeo Beach, helping restore native buckwheat and lizardtail communities that stabilize soils and feed native pollinators.
fullDescription: South African ice plant (Carpobrotus edulis) has spread across thousands of acres of California coastal bluffs, displacing the native coastal scrub communities that evolved here. This one-day volunteer event at the Marin Headlands focuses on manually removing ice plant mats from a 2-acre bluff section overlooking Rodeo Beach. Work involves pulling, rolling, and stacking ice plant mats — physically satisfying if tiring work. Conservancy ecologists will lead an introduction to coastal bluff ecology and native plant identification before the crew gets to work. All tools, gloves, and sunscreen provided. Stunning coastal views.
nextSteps: Register at parksconservancy.org/volunteer. Limited to 25 volunteers. Rodeo Beach parking lot is the meeting point.

title: Bay Shoreline Bioblitz Volunteer
description: Join a one-day biodiversity blitz at Point Pinole Regional Shoreline, documenting plants, invertebrates, birds, and fish to build a snapshot of Bay shoreline health.
fullDescription: Save the Bay is partnering with iNaturalist and the California Academy of Sciences to conduct a day-long bioblitz at Point Pinole Regional Shoreline. Volunteer teams spread out across designated habitat zones — mudflat, salt marsh, grassland, and riparian — photographing and recording every species they encounter. No prior expertise required; staff naturalists and app-based AI identification tools support all participants. Observations are uploaded to iNaturalist in real time, contributing to a Bay Area biodiversity baseline dataset. Children age 8 and older are welcome with a parent. The event concludes with a species tally and prize raffle.
nextSteps: Register at savesfbay.org/bioblitz. Download the iNaturalist app before arriving. All skill levels welcome.

title: Mount Tam Interpretive Trail Guide
description: Lead public interpretive hikes on Mt. Tamalpais, sharing natural and cultural history with visitors from around the world on one of the Bay Area's most beloved mountains.
fullDescription: One Tam's volunteer interpretive guide program trains passionate nature lovers to lead monthly public hikes on Mt. Tamalpais. Guides develop and lead 2–3 hour walks on routes like the Matt Davis Trail, Steep Ravine, and the East Peak summit circuit, weaving together stories of the mountain's ecology, Indigenous Miwok history, and conservation legacy. A 24-hour training program covers natural history content, public facilitation skills, and Leave No Trace principles. Guides are expected to lead at least one hike per month during the program season (April–October). An extraordinary way to deepen your own knowledge while sharing the mountain you love.
nextSteps: Apply for the spring guide training at onetam.org/volunteer by March 15. Training takes place over three weekends in April.

title: South Bay Wetland Water Quality Monitor
description: Monitor water quality and wildlife at Sunnyvale Baylands, collecting dissolved oxygen, salinity, and temperature data that helps track wetland recovery after decades of industrial salt pond use.
fullDescription: The South Bay Salt Pond Restoration Project is the largest tidal wetland restoration effort on the West Coast. Acterra coordinates a citizen science monitoring network that tracks water quality as former industrial salt ponds transition back to functional wetland habitat. Volunteer monitors visit assigned pond stations monthly (or more frequently if desired) to collect field measurements using handheld instruments and observe wildlife activity. Data is entered into an online portal and reviewed by Acterra ecologists. Monitors must complete a two-hour field training and commit to a minimum of six visits over six months. Excellent birding along the way — American avocets, stilts, and dunlin are common.
nextSteps: Sign up for a field training session at acterra.org/volunteer. Trainings offered monthly on weekday mornings.
